records.relevance: Within 4000 flags, chiral 4-polytopes with dodecahedral facets exist: type [4,3,5] order 1320 (dual {5,3,4}: 22 dodecahedral facets, 55 vertices - computed by me from the relations) and type [5,3,6] order 1920 (32 dodecahedral facets, 20 vertices). A chiral 4-polytope of type {30,3,3} with facet R97.9 (2880 flags) would need >= 2880*3 = 8640 flags by Conder's inequality (see Fields-slides record), so it cannot appear; likewise for R151.11 (>= 2400*3 = 7200 flags) and for the {30,3,3} candidate with group order 7200 (14400 flags).

records.title: Two atlases of abstract chiral polytopes for small groups
records.authors: Michael I. Hartley, Isabel Hubard, Dimitri Leemans
records.how_found: Web search; article page fetched; PDF downloaded and text-extracted with PyPDF2.
records.theorem_or_page: Abstract; Theorem 3.1; Section 5 and Table 1 (p. 376); Table 4
records.verbatim_quote: Abstract: 'We construct chiral abstract polytopes in two different ways. Firstly we seek them as quotients of regular polytopes arising from the Atlas of Small Regular Polytopes (http://www.abstract-polytopes.com/atlas/); the resulting atlas of chiral polytopes atlas is available on the website http://www.abstract-polytopes.com/chiral/. Secondly, for each almost simple group Γ such that S ≤ Γ ≤ Aut(S) where S is a simple group and Γ is a group of order less than 900,000 listed in the Atlas of Finite Groups, we give, up to isomorphism, the number of abstract chiral polytopes on which Γ acts regularly.' Theorem 3.1: 'The polytope Q = P/N is chiral if and only if N_Γ(P)(N) has index 2 in Γ(P), and contains none of the generators ρ0,...,ρn−1.' Section 5: 'In the first atlas, in total, 56 chiral polytopes were discovered, 48 of rank 3, and 8 of rank 4.' Table 1 (Rank 4 chiral quotients Q of small regular polytopes): '{3,3,8}*768b   ((Q8 × 2) ⋊ 2) ⋊ S4   Q8 ⋊ S4' ; '{3,6,9}*972a   3^3 ⋊ (D9 × 2)   (3^3 ⋊ 3) ⋊ 2' ; '{3,6,18}*1944a ...' ; '{6,6,9}*1944a ...'. Table 4 row: 'PGL(2,11)  PGL(2,11)  1320  78  24 = 0 + 24' (i.e. 24 chiral polytopes of rank 4, none of rank 3).
records.relevance: Confirms the {8,3,3} chiral polytope with group Q8 ⋊ S4 (order 192) is the unique rank-4 chiral polytope of that type with regular cover in Hartley's atlas. The PGL(2,11) row (order 1320, 24 rank-4 chiral polytopes) is consistent with Conder's [4,3,5]-entry of order 1320 with dodecahedral (dual) facets, but that identification was not verified.

records.title: Chiral extensions of chiral polytopes
records.how_found: Web search; arXiv abs page fetched; arXiv PDF downloaded and text-extracted; DOI from Crossref.
records.theorem_or_page: Abstract; Theorem 1 (p. 2); Lemma 3; Theorem 8; Theorem 10 (Section 4); Theorem 11, Theorem 14, Corollary 15 (Section 5)
records.verbatim_quote: Abstract: 'Given a chiral d-polytope K with regular facets, we describe a construction for a chiral (d+1)-polytope P with facets isomorphic to K. Furthermore, P is finite whenever K is finite. We provide explicit examples of chiral 4-polytopes constructed in this way from chiral toroidal maps.' Intro: 'An important partial result was given in [12], where it is shown how to build a finite chiral polytope of rank d+1 with facets isomorphic to a finite regular polytope K of rank d. There are very restrictive conditions on the polytope K, however, so more work remains to be done even on this piece of the extension problem (Problem 27 of [13]).' 'Theorem 1 Every finite chiral d-polytope with regular facets is itself the facet of a finite chiral (d+1)-polytope. This gives a partial answer to Problem 26 in [13]. We note that the assumption that the chiral d-polytope has regular facets is necessary (see [16, Proposition 9]).' 'Theorem 10 The graph G_P defined above is a GPR graph of a chiral (d+1)-polytope with facets isomorphic to K.' 'Theorem 10 does not require the polytope K to be finite. However, in [18] another construction was given of an infinite chiral (d+1)-polytope whose facets are any given chiral d-polytope with regular facets.' 'Theorem 11 Let K, σ1, σ2 and τ be defined as in the preceding discussion, with n = b^2+c^2 prime. Let Γ = ⟨σ1,σ2,τ⟩. Then Γ is the automorphism group of a finite chiral polytope with Schläfli symbol {4,4,2(n−2)} and facets isomorphic to K.' 'Theorem 14 ... Then Γ(P) ≅ (A_n × A_n) ⋊ D4.' Concluding remark: 'other possible definitions of τ ... may yield 4-polytopes with smaller automorphism groups Γ. However, the determination of Γ in such a general setting involves bigger complications and is out of the scope of this paper.'
records.relevance: The general finite chiral-extension theorem applies to CHIRAL facets with regular facets (rank >= 4 output from a chiral polyhedron K), not to regular facets such as {5,3}, {8,3}*96, R97.9. For regular facets the only general tool cited is Pellicer 2010 with 'very restrictive conditions'. The last Schläfli entry of the extension is not controlled here (e.g. 2(n-2)).

records.title: A construction of higher rank chiral polytopes
records.how_found: Web search; abstract retrieved from Semantic Scholar API (ScienceDirect returned 403). Full text not retrieved; theorem numbers not retrieved.
records.verbatim_quote: Abstract: 'In this paper we describe a construction for chiral polytopes with preassigned regular facets. Furthermore we show that this construction implies the existence of chiral d-polytopes, for every rank d>=3.' Pellicer 2012 (AMC) describes it: 'The only known general result in this direction is given in [49], where chiral extensions were found for minimal regular covers of the so-called scattered chiral polytopes. This was used to provide a recursive construction of chiral polytopes of all ranks higher than 3. However, very few polytopes are regular covers of scattered chiral polytopes.' Cunningham-Pellicer 2014 refer to it via 'Lemma 1', 'Proposition 7' and 'Theorem 3.7' of [12].
records.relevance: The only published general construction of chiral (d+1)-polytopes with PRESCRIBED REGULAR facets; hypotheses (facet must be the minimal regular cover of a 'scattered' chiral polytope) are restrictive and would need to be checked for {5,3}, {8,3}*96, {12,3}*288, {12,4}*384e, R97.9, R151.11. Conder's slides: 'Daniel Pellicer's proof involved a construction for chiral polytopes with prescribed regular facets. But these can be very large!'

records.title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
records.how_found: Cited by Cunningham-Pellicer as [13]; AMC page fetched, PDF downloaded and text-extracted.
records.verbatim_quote: 'In [53] it was proved that for every regular d-polytope K there exists a universal regular extension U(K) ... The equivalent result for chiral polytopes was established in [59]. Specifically, it was established that every chiral d-polytope K with regular facets admits a universal chiral extension U^ch(K) ... However, it is not known yet whether there exists a chiral polytope covering all other chiral extensions of a regular polytope K.' 'Problem 24 Determine whether for every (any) regular polytope K there exists a chiral extension which covers every extension of K.' 'Little is known about chiral extensions of regular or chiral polytopes. The main result in this direction is the construction of U^ch(K) given in [59].' 'Problem 25 Does every chiral polytope K with regular facets admit a chiral extension with prescribed last entry of the Schläfli symbol?' 'Problem 26 Does every chiral finite polytope K with regular facets admit a finite chiral extension with prescribed last entry of the Schläfli symbol?' 'A necessary condition for a regular polytope to admit chiral extensions is orientability.' 'Problem 27 Does every orientably regular d-polytope admit a chiral extension (d ≥ 2)?' 'Problem 28 Does every orientably regular finite d-polytope admit a finite chiral extension (d ≥ 2)?' 'Problem 29 Does every orientably regular polytope admit an infinite chiral extension?' 'Problem 30 Does every convex regular polytope admit a chiral extensions?' 'Problem 37 Classify all finite and infinite chiral k-polytopes in R^d (where k < d ...' 'Problem 38 Classify all finite chiral polyhedra in E^4.' 'Problem 39 Classify all infinite chiral 4-polytopes in E^4.'
records.relevance: States precisely the open status (as of 2012) of the abstract question: whether an orientably regular polytope (e.g. the maps {8,3}*96, {12,4}*384e, {12,3}*288, R97.9, R151.11, or {5,3}) admits a (finite) chiral extension. Also lists the geometric classification problems in E^4.

records.title: Chiral polytopes
records.venue: Applied Geometry and Discrete Mathematics (The Victor Klee Festschrift), DIMACS Series in Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science 4, AMS (1991), pp. 493-516
records.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1090/dimacs/004/39 (DOI from Crossref); AMS page https://www.ams.org/books/dimacs/004/39 returned HTTP 403
records.how_found: Crossref bibliographic search; Weiss's York publication list (https://weiss.info.yorku.ca/articles/) confirms bibliographic data; no open PDF found. Full text NOT retrieved; Section 6 Theorems 2 and 3 NOT retrieved.
records.theorem_or_page: Theorem 1 and Proposition 9 as cited by Conder-Hubard-Pisanski 2008 and Cunningham-Pellicer 2014 (statements paraphrased by those papers)
records.verbatim_quote: Conder-Hubard-Pisanski, p. 5: 'Conversely, if Γ is any permutation group generated by elements σ1,σ2,...,σn−1 which satisfy the relations (3) and the intersection condition, then there exists a polytope P of rank n which is either directly regular or chiral, of type {p1,...,pn−1} where pi is the order of σi ... Moreover, P is directly regular if and only if there exists an involutory group automorphism ρ : Γ → Γ such that ρ(σ1) = σ1^{-1}, ρ(σ2) = σ1^2 σ2, and ρ(σi) = σi for 3 ≤ i ≤ n−1 ...; see [23, Theorem 1]).' Cunningham-Pellicer: 'The facets and vertex-figures of a chiral polytope must be either orientably regular or chiral, and the (d−2)-faces must be orientably regular (see [16, Proposition 9]).' CHP on universal polytopes: 'In fact this is the universal 4-polytope having such facets and vertex figures ... so is isomorphic to the universal {{4,4}(2,1),{4,4}(1,2)} 4-polytope; see [23].'
records.relevance: Foundational group-theoretic characterisation used to decide whether a candidate rotation group (e.g. [3,3,5]^+ of order 7200 with the H_0({5,3,3}) facet group) is the group of a chiral 4-polytope: relations + intersection condition, and chirality iff no such involutory automorphism ρ exists. The exact text of Theorems 2-3 (Section 6, universal {P1,P2}^ch) could not be retrieved.

Finite extensions receive discussion as well.' Schulte's Fields slides: 'Extension problem: Chiral n-polytope P as the facet of a chiral (n+1)-polytope Q? Facets of P regular! (a) Universal: Γ(Q) ≅ Γ(P) *_{Γ+(F)} Γ(F) (Weiss & S., 1994) (b) Finite Q, if P is finite. (Cunningham & Pellicer, 2013)'.
records.relevance: The universal (infinite) chiral extension exists only for CHIRAL polytopes with regular facets; for a REGULAR facet K the analogous universal object is the regular U(K) (Pellicer 2012: 'In this sense, U^ch(K) does not exist for regular K').

records.title: Constructions for chiral polytopes
records.authors: Marston Conder, Isabel Hubard, Tomaž Pisanski
records.venue: Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2) 77 (1) (2008) 115-129
records.how_found: Web search; Crossref for bibliographic data; preprint PDF downloaded and text-extracted.
records.theorem_or_page: Abstract; Section 2 (history); Section 3 (p. 5); Sections on smallest chiral 4-polytopes (Figs. 5, 7) and 5-polytopes
records.verbatim_quote: Abstract: 'In this paper, we describe a method for constructing finite chiral n-polytopes, by seeking particular normal subgroups of the orientation-preserving subgroup of n-generator Coxeter group ... This technique is used to identify the smallest examples of chiral 3- and 4-polytopes, in both the self-dual and non self-dual cases, and then to give the first known examples of finite chiral 5-polytopes'. History: 'In 1970 Coxeter [8] used honeycombs to construct a family of chiral 4-polytopes, by forcing the right and left Petrie motions of the polytopes to have different lengths. Later Schulte and Weiss [24] constructed examples from hyperbolic honeycombs, using isometries of hyperbolic 3-space and complex Mobius transformations. Also Nostrand [19] has constructed such chiral 4-polytopes whose faces are cubes or dodecahedra.' Smallest chiral 4-polytopes: self-dual of type {4,4,4}: 'All the facets and vertex figures of this 4-polytope are isomorphic to the chiral 3-polytope associated with the chiral map {4,4}(1,2) ... isomorphic to the universal {{4,4}(2,1),{4,4}(1,2)} 4-polytope'; non-self-dual of type {3,4,4}: 'the facets are all isomorphic to the regular 3-polytope of type {3,4} ... In fact this 4-polytope is isomorphic to the universal {{3,4},{4,4}(1,2)} 4-polytope.'
records.relevance: Method (normal subgroups of the rotation subgroup of a Coxeter group not normalised by reflections) is exactly what a search for a chiral {30,3,3} or {8,3,3} with prescribed facet group would use; the paper contains no example with facets {5,3}, {8,3}*96, {12,3}, {12,4}, {30,3} or {20,5}. Attributes chiral 4-polytopes with dodecahedral facets to Nostrand.

records.title: Chiral polytopes from hyperbolic honeycombs
records.authors: B. Nostrand, E. Schulte (NB: not Schulte-Weiss; year 1995, not 1994)

records.title: Chirality and projective linear groups
records.how_found: Web search (ScienceDirect snippet); Crossref record; ScienceDirect page 403.
records.verbatim_quote: Snippet of abstract: 'The correspondence of groups and polytopes is used to construct infinite series of chiral and regular polytopes whose facets or vertex-figures are chiral or regular toroidal maps. In particular, the groups PSL2(Zm) are used to construct chiral polytopes, while PSL2(Zm[i]) and PSL2(Zm[ω]) are used to construct regular polytopes.' records.title: Constructions of Chiral Polytopes of Small Rank
records.authors: Antonio Breda D'Azevedo, Gareth A. Jones, Egon Schulte
records.venue: Canadian Journal of Mathematics 63 (2011) 1254-1283 (per Cunningham-Pellicer ref [1]); arXiv:1008.1080 (5 Aug 2010)
records.how_found: Web search for locally spherical chiral 4-polytopes; arXiv PDF downloaded and text-extracted.
records.theorem_or_page: Section 7 'Locally spherical polytopes': Theorems 7.1, 7.2, 7.3 (pp. 18-19 of arXiv v1)
records.verbatim_quote: 'Theorem 7.1 Let p be a prime, let p ≡ ±1 mod 5 or p = 5, and let Q be a finite locally spherical directly regular 4-polytope of type {5,3,5} such that p(p^2−1) does not divide |Γ(Q)|. Then there exists a locally spherical chiral 4-polytope of type {5,3,5} with group L2(p) × Γ+(Q).' 'For instance, let Q be the classical regular star-polytope {5/2,3,5} (of type {5,3,5}) in euclidean 4-space ... Hence Theorem 7.1 applies (if p ≠ 5) and yields locally spherical chiral 4-polytopes of type {5,3,5} with groups isomorphic to L2(p) × H4^+.' 'Theorem 7.2 ... Then there exists a locally spherical chiral 4-polytope of type {3,5,3} with group L2(p) × Γ+(Q).' 'Theorem 7.3 Let p be a prime with p ≡ ±1 or ±9 mod 40, with either 1+√5 or 1−√5 a square mod p. Let Q be a finite locally spherical directly regular 4-polytope of type {5,3,4} such that p(p^2−1) does not divide |Γ(Q)|. Then there exists a locally spherical chiral 4-polytope of type {5,3,4} with group L2(p) × Γ+(Q).'
records.relevance: Explicit infinite families of finite chiral 4-polytopes with dodecahedral facets {5,3} (types {5,3,5} and {5,3,4}); shows the abstract question for facet {5,3} has a positive answer in the literature (finite, with vertex-figures {3,5} or {3,4}).

records.title: On the Schläfli symbol of chiral extensions of polytopes
records.how_found: Web search; arXiv abs fetched; DOI via Crossref.
records.verbatim_quote: 'Given an abstract n-polytope K, an abstract (n+1)-polytope P is an extension of K if all the facets of P are isomorphic to K. A chiral polytope is a polytope with maximal rotational symmetry that does not admit any reflections. If P is a chiral extension of K, then all but the last entry of the Schläfli symbol of P are determined. In this paper we introduce some constructions of chiral extensions P of certain chiral polytopes in such a way that the last entry of the Schläfli symbol of P is arbitrarily large.'
records.relevance: Addresses Pellicer's Problems 25/26 (last Schläfli entry) for CHIRAL K; not for regular facets.

records.title: Chiral extensions of regular toroids
records.authors: Antonio Montero, Micael Toledo (NB: not Cunningham-Pellicer)
records.how_found: Web search; Springer page redirected (not fetched); Semantic Scholar API and arXiv abs fetched.
records.verbatim_quote: 'In this paper we build chiral polytopes whose facets (maximal faces) are isomorphic to a prescribed regular cubic tessellation of the n-dimensional torus (n ≥ 2). As a consequence, we prove that for every d ≥ 3 there exist infinitely many chiral d-polytopes.' Related talk abstract (Pellicer, CMS Winter 2018, https://www2.cms.math.ca/Events/winter18/res/pdf/dcg-dp.pdf): 'it is still not known whether a given regular polytope of rank n is the facet of a chiral polytope of rank n+1. In this talk I will present a construction that shows that all but finitely many regular toroidal polytopes of rank n and type {4,3^{n−3},4} are facets of chiral polytopes of rank n+1.'
records.relevance: Most recent general result on chiral extensions of REGULAR facets, but only for cubic toroids {4,3^{n-3},4}; the 2018 talk abstract states explicitly that the general question for a given regular facet was open.

records.verbatim_quote: '[Joint work with Dimitri Leemans (2012/13)] We now have complete lists of all regular polytopes with up to 4000 flags and all chiral polytopes with up to 4000 flags. ... if P is a regular/chiral polytope of type {k1,k2,...,kn−1}, and its facets have m flags, then P has at least m·kn−1 flags. Up to 4000 flags, the largest rank for regular is 6, and the largest rank for chiral is 5.' 'Theorem [Daniel Pellicer (2010)]: For every d ≥ 3, there exists a finite chiral polytope of rank d. It is easy to prove that if P is a chiral polytope of rank d, then its sub-polytopes of rank d−2 are regular (not chiral), so a recursive construction is impossible. Daniel Pellicer's proof involved a construction for chiral polytopes with prescribed regular facets. But these can be very large!' 'Theorem [Hubard, O'Reilly-Regueiro, Pellicer & MC] For all but finitely many n, there exists a chiral 4-polytope P of type {3,3,k} for some k, with Aut P = Alt(n) or Sym(n).'

records.theorem_or_page: Chapter 6 summary; Chapter 5 summary; Chapter 4 summary; book blurb
records.verbatim_quote: Chapter 6 summary: 'Abstract chiral polytopes are intrinsically combinatorial objects. In this chapter a geometric meaning is given to many of them. This follows the ideas of Grünbaum of skeletal polyhedra. As part of the discussion, chiral polyhedra in Euclidean three-dimensional space are described in a different way from the one in which they were originally found by Schulte. Chiral polytopes of full rank are those that attain a certain upper bound with respect to their dimensions; this is the same bound used to define regular polytopes of full rank. It is proven that chiral polytopes of full rank exist only in ranks 4 and 5. This is an unexpected contrast with regular polytopes of full rank, which exist in every rank.' Chapter 4 summary: 'The idea of this chapter is to show ways to construct polytopes from other polytopes, with emphasis on constructions yielding chiral polytopes ... The last construction, called the mix, uses two polytopes to obtain a third polytope that covers the other two.' Chapter 5 summary (fetch-tool paraphrase): covers chiral polyhedra, tight chiral polytopes, examples from geometry including 'Coxeter's twisted honeycombs and Roli's cube', and constructions of high-rank chiral polytopes by 'amalgamation' and 'extensions'. Blurb: 'featuring examples, exercises, figures, and 75 open problems' (paraphrase).
records.relevance: The current reference monograph (2025); its skeletal chapter and 75 open problems are the most likely place where the PETCOX-facet extension question is stated as open, but Appendix C could not be read.

Schulte, DCG 13 (1995) 17-39, DOI 10.1007/BF02574026 - not Schulte-Weiss 1994; the Schulte-Weiss 1994 paper is 'Chirality and projective linear groups', Discrete Math. 131, 221-261. (2) 'Chiral extensions of regular toroids' (Combinatorica, DOI 10.1007/s00493-024-00132-0, arXiv 2405.09434) is by Montero and Toledo, not Cunningham-Pellicer. (3) Conder's regular-maps file is RegularOrientableMaps301.txt (the task's OrientableRegularMaps301.txt is 404). (4) Cunningham-Pellicer 2014 is arXiv 1307.7007, DOI 10.1016/j.disc.2014.04.014. Key take-aways for the research question: the published general extension theorems (Schulte-Weiss 1995 universal U^ch(K); Cunningham-Pellicer 2014 finite extension; Montero 2021) all require the facet K to be CHIRAL with regular facets, so they do not apply to regular facets such as H_0({5,3,3}) (whose map is R97.9, group 2880/rotations 1440), {8,3}*96, {12,4}*384e, {12,3}*288, R151.11 or {5,3}. For regular facets the only general tools are Pellicer 2010 (restrictive hypotheses, not verified from primary text) and Montero-Toledo 2024 (cubic toroids only); Pellicer 2012 Problems 27-28 ('Does every orientably regular (finite) d-polytope admit a (finite) chiral extension?') and Pellicer's 2018 talk abstract state the question as open. Existence of chiral 4-polytopes with dodecahedral facets is settled positively in the literature: Breda D'Azevedo-Jones-Schulte Theorems 7.1/7.3 (types {5,3,5}, {5,3,4}), Nostrand-Schulte 1995 (per CHP: 'faces are cubes or dodecahedra'), and in Conder's 4000-flag census (type [4,3,5] order 1320, dual {5,3,4}; type [5,3,6] order 1920). Roli's cube type {8,3,3}: Conder's census entry 'group of order 192, NSD, Type [3,3,8]' and the chiral atlas {8,3,3} with regular cover {8,3,3}*768b and group Q8 ⋊ S4 (order 192) are the only abstract chiral polytopes of that type below 2000 flags (a second, order 768, below 4000); my GAP check confirms the order-192 one has facets isomorphic (as maps) to {8,3}*96, with 4 facets and 16 vertices - identification with Roli's cube itself was not verified against BHP 2014. My own GAP computation (flagged as such, medium confidence) further found within Conder's census: facets {8,3}*96 also in chiral polytopes of types {8,3,6} (8 entries, orders 384-1536) and {8,3,12} (2 entries, order 768); facets {12,3}*288 in exactly one chiral polytope, type {12,3,4}, order 1152 (8 facets, 48 vertices); facets {12,4}*384e in three, types {12,4,3} (order 1152) and {12,4,4} (orders 960, 1920). No census entry can have facets R97.9 or R151.11 (flag bound). The 2000-flag list's WebFetch summary initially claimed 'no rank-4 entries'; this was a summarizer error corrected by inspecting the raw file - the parent should treat any summarizer-only claim with caution.
